## After this lecture you can

- turn raw text into model-ready units, and defend each preprocessing choice
- explain byte-pair encoding well enough to predict how a tokenizer splits an unseen word
- describe Zipf's law and its practical consequence, the vocabulary problem
- derive a TF-IDF vector by hand and get the same numbers as `scikit-learn`
- say precisely what bag-of-words can and cannot represent
- explain why tokenization is where multilingual pain — including Turkish morphology — begins

::: {.notes}
These are the chapter's learning objectives. The fifth one continues in the book:
"and defend that in an interview" — interview questions close today's lecture.

The route follows the chapter. First the units: how a string becomes tokens, why
every way of cutting it is wrong in some direction, and who pays for that in
Turkish. Then a detour through Zipf's law, which explains why the vocabulary
never stops growing. Then the core — six steps that take four short sentences
all the way to vectors you can measure distances on, with every intermediate
number shown. Then what this representation cannot do, which is the reason the
next chapter exists, and a real experiment on whether any of it still matters.

Every number in the chapter was produced by running the code shown, with
scikit-learn 1.9, tiktoken 0.13, sentencepiece 0.2.2 and tokenizers 0.22.
:::

## The problem, in one sentence

::: {.lede}
A model is a function that does arithmetic on numbers. Text is a string of characters.
:::

A model cannot compute with letters; text has to become numbers first. The bridge from text to numbers has two spans:

1. [decide what the units are]{.hl} — **tokenization**
2. [decide what number each unit contributes]{.hl} — **weighting**

::: {.takeaway}
Preprocessing is not preparation for the model. Preprocessing *is part of* the model — every choice below is a modelling assumption, and it belongs in your methods section.
:::

::: {.notes}
That is the whole chapter.

Say it up front, because the techniques below — bag-of-words, TF-IDF — are
sometimes dismissed as historical. They are not. They are the sparse half of a
field whose dense half students meet in Chapter 3 (Embeddings). They still win
on small data, they still power production search, and interviews for applied
NLP roles routinely probe whether you understand them.

More importantly: building these simple representations forces a series of
*decisions* on you. Which units do you cut the text into? Which differences do
you erase? What do you count and what do you throw away? A system built on a
large language model makes the same decisions today. There they are buried
inside a ready-made tokenizer or library. Here you make each one yourself, so
you can see it.

The statistician's framing in the takeaway is the chapter's margin note, and it
serves for the whole lecture.
:::

## Split on whitespace — and watch it fail

```python
text = "The pump P-101 didn't fail; it's the seal (again!)."
print(text.split())
```

```text
['The', 'pump', 'P-101', "didn't", 'fail;', "it's", 'the', 'seal', '(again!).']
```

- `fail;` and `fail` are now different tokens. So are `The` and `the`, and `it's` and `it is`
- Each fix either merges things that should stay apart, or splits things that should stay together
- [The ways this fails are the entire design space of tokenization]{.hl}
- What fails is **naive whitespace tokenization**; a serious word tokenizer handles punctuation, apostrophes and URLs — what it cannot fix is the open vocabulary

::: {.notes}
Before a model can count anything, something has to decide what a *thing* is.
That decision is yours, you make it once, and everything downstream inherits
it: how large the vocabulary grows, what counts as a word the model has never
seen, and — if a vendor bills you per token — what a sentence costs.

Nobody announces this decision; it arrives disguised as a one-line call to a
library. This section is about making it on purpose.

Vocabulary: *tokenization* is cutting a run of text into the pieces the model
will count; what counts as a piece is a design decision, not a fact about
language. A *token* is one of those pieces — often a word, sometimes part of a
word, sometimes punctuation. When a vendor charges "per token", this is the
thing being counted.
:::

## The normalization ladder {.smaller}

| Step | [What it buys you]{.pro} | [What it costs you]{.con} | Default |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Lowercasing** | `Pump` = `pump`, halving many counts | `US` → `us`, `Apple` → `apple`; in Turkish `str.lower()` is silently wrong | Yes for English; Turkish and Azerbaijani need a locale-aware conversion |
| **Punctuation stripping** | `fail;` = `fail` | Destroys `P-101`, decimals, URLs, chemical formulas | No — strip selectively |
| **Stop word removal** | drops `the`, `is`, `of`: 43.9% of tokens here | Destroys negation (`not`), and *to be or not to be* | Only for sparse count models |
| **Stemming** | `replaced` → `replac`, cheaply | Crude suffix chopping: `university` → `univers` = `universe` | No |
| **Lemmatization** | `replaced` → `replace`, correctly | Needs a dictionary and part-of-speech tagging; slow | Rarely — subwords are cheaper |

::: {.takeaway}
Read the table's last column with suspicion: what it holds is a default, not a rule. [Try both and measure.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The example on the previous slide left three decisions: should `The` and `the`
count as one word, should the semicolon go, should `it's` and `it is` be
merged? All three are the same kind: erase the difference between two
spellings, or keep it. Normalization is deliberately erasing differences you
have decided not to care about. Why not erase as many as possible? Because
every step also destroys something, and you do not find out what until later. The table gives the
argument *against* each step — because the arguments against are what
interviewers actually ask about.

Every step is a bet that the distinction it erases does not matter for *your*
task. Lowercasing is usually free in topic classification and removes a useful
cue in named entity recognition (NER), where capitalisation is part of the
signal.

Stemming and lemmatization aim at the same thing — collapsing inflected forms —
but they are not the same operation. Stemming (Porter 1980) applies rewrite
rules and does not care whether the result is a word. Lemmatization returns the
dictionary form — the form you would look the word up under, the infinitive of
a verb or the uninflected form of a noun — and needs to know that `left` is the
past tense of `leave` in one sentence and a direction in another.

The modern answer to "which should I use?" depends on the pipeline. Feeding a
pretrained transformer: use the model's own tokenizer and do neither — subwords
already handle the rare-word half of what stemming was for. But subwords split a
rare word into pieces; they do not collapse `kullanıyorum` and `kullandık` into
one shared column. Where you need that — lexical search, a sparse classifier,
anything counting term matches — a stemmer still does real work: Chapter 16
(Turkish and Morphologically Rich Languages) measures it taking Turkish
recall@1 from 28.0% to 95.3%.
:::

## Two steps sold as free

### Lowercasing depends on the language

```python
"İSTANBUL".lower()              # 'i̇stanbul' — 'i' + U+0307, nine characters
"İSTANBUL".lower() == "istanbul"  # False
"IĞDIR".lower()                 # 'iğdir' — should be 'ığdır'
```

- Nothing errors. The result lands in a different vocabulary column from the word a user types — forever

### Stop word removal deletes nearly half your text

- `scikit-learn`'s English list: 318 words, [0.4% of the vocabulary but 43.9% of all tokens]{.hl} — a compression win for a sparse model, a catastrophe if the signal is in *not*

::: {.notes}
This is the first mention of Unicode; introduce it in one sentence: the shared
table that gives every letter and sign of every writing system a number (`A`
is 65, `ç` is 231, `İ` is 304). The detail comes a few slides later.

Python's `str.lower()` implements the Unicode *default* case mapping — the
language-independent one. The standard defines language-specific tailorings
alongside it, and does not apply them unless you ask. Turkish needs a tailoring,
because it has two `i` letters and two `I` letters.

Chapter 4 (A Representation Bake-Off) hits this bug on a real corpus, and
Chapter 16 gives the locale-aware fix. The point here is only that
"lowercasing" is a language-dependent operation being presented as a free one.

The stop word numbers are measured on the corpus used later in the chapter. A *stop word* is a word so common that some pipelines throw it away
before counting — *the*, *of*, *is*. Whether that is a saving or a mistake
depends entirely on the task.
:::

## One word at three unit sizes

Suppose `unbreakable` never appeared in the training text:

| Unit | How `unbreakable` looks | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Word** | `<UNK>` | [Not in the vocabulary: the model gets nothing but the "unknown word" marker]{.con} |
| **Character** | `u` `n` `b` `r` `e` `a` `k` `a` `b` `l` `e` | [Nothing is lost, but one word became 11 units, and `u` on its own says nothing]{.con} |
| **Subword** | `un` `break` `able` | [3 units, each familiar from other words: `undo`, `breaking`, `readable`]{.pro} |

::: {.takeaway}
Who chose `un`, `break` and `able`? [Nobody did. They were found by counting.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.src}
Last row: how the `cl100k_base` tokenizer actually splits this word
:::

::: {.notes}
Word-level tokenization has a problem it cannot solve on its own: the
vocabulary never closes. Character-level tokenization has the opposite problem:
sequences become very long and each unit means almost nothing. Subwords are the
middle road.

This slide shows the three options on one word instead of describing them in
the abstract. The split in the last row is not made up; OpenAI's `cl100k_base`
tokenizer cuts `unbreakable` exactly there.

The question that leads to the next slide: who chose those pieces? The answer
is byte-pair encoding.
:::

## Byte-pair encoding: count, merge, repeat

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="35%"}
1. Start with characters
2. Count every adjacent pair
3. Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol
4. Repeat

A four-word corpus: `low` ×5, `lower` ×2, `newest` ×6, `widest` ×3

[Nobody told it that English has suffixes.]{.hl} It counted.
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
```text
merge  1: 'e' + 's' -> 'es'  (seen 9 times)
merge  2: 'es' + 't' -> 'est'  (seen 9 times)
merge  3: 'est' + '</w>' -> 'est</w>'  (seen 9 times)
merge  4: 'l' + 'o' -> 'lo'  (seen 7 times)
merge  5: 'lo' + 'w' -> 'low'  (seen 7 times)
merge  6: 'n' + 'e' -> 'ne'  (seen 6 times)
merge  7: 'ne' + 'w' -> 'new'  (seen 6 times)
merge  8: 'new' + 'est</w>' -> 'newest</w>'  (seen 6 times)
merge  9: 'low' + '</w>' -> 'low</w>'  (seen 5 times)
merge 10: 'w' + 'i' -> 'wi'  (seen 3 times)
```
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Sennrich et al. 2016
:::

::: {.notes}
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is how the middle road of the previous slide is found:
it *learns* its units from data (Sennrich et al. 2016).

`</w>` marks the end of a word. Look at what happened without anyone supplying a
grammar. The first two merges build `est` — the English superlative suffix — and
the third attaches the word boundary to it, because superlatives are frequent.
It discovered `low` and `new` as stems.

The book shows the full merge loop in Python, and an interactive widget where
you type a word and watch the merges apply. Only 10 merges were learned
here, from a four-word corpus; a real tokenizer learns 50,000 or more.
:::

## A word it has never seen

```text
lowest   -> low est</w>
newer    -> new e r </w>
slow     -> s low</w>
widest   -> wi d est</w>
```

- To tokenize, replay the learned merges in the order they were learned
- `lowest` never appeared in training, and it is still cut into two pieces the model knows
- [As long as every character of a word is in the alphabet, an unseen *word* does not become `<UNK>`]{.hl}: in the worst case it is cut into shorter pieces
- Notice the condition: an unseen *character* still breaks this example. `çay` → `('ç', 'a', 'y', '</w>')`, none of them in the vocabulary

::: {.notes}
This is the main reason subwords won: in the worst case a word is cut into
shorter pieces. Representation quality drops; the input does not become
unrepresentable.

State the condition out loud: every *character* of the new word has to be in
the alphabet the merges were learned over. Ours came from `low`, `lower`,
`newest` and `widest` only. So `apply_merges("çay", merges)` returns characters
that are not in the vocabulary at all.

This is where real tokenizers differ from this small example. The next three
slides take it up: first the terms character, Unicode and byte; then starting
from bytes; then byte fallback.
:::

## Character, ASCII, Unicode, byte

- **ASCII** (1963): 128 numbers for the English letters, digits and punctuation. No `ç`, `ş` or `ğ`
- **Unicode**: one number for every character of every writing system — its **code point**
- **Byte**: a number from 0 to 255. **UTF-8** writes each code point as 1 to 4 bytes

| | `ç` | `a` | `y` |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Unicode code point | 231 (U+00E7) | 97 (U+0061) | 121 (U+0079) |
| In the ASCII table? | no | yes | yes |
| UTF-8 bytes | 195, 167 | 97 | 121 |

::: {.takeaway}
`çay` (tea): three letters to you, three numbers to Unicode, [four bytes on disk.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Students mix these four words up all the time, which is why they get a slide.

A character is a letter or sign as you see it on screen. A computer cannot
store letters, only numbers, so every character needs a number. ASCII is the
first widely used table that assigns them. Unicode is the same idea extended to
every writing system; the 128 ASCII characters keep their numbers in Unicode
(`a` is still 97).

A byte is the basic unit a computer stores data in: eight bits, 256 different
values. Unicode's numbers go far beyond 255, so a character does not always fit
in one byte. An encoding decides which bytes store a code point. UTF-8 writes 0
to 127, the ASCII characters, as a single byte and larger numbers as two, three
or four bytes.

You can show it in Python: `len("çay")` is 3, `len("çay".encode("utf-8"))` is 4.
:::

## Characters or bytes: what BPE starts from

::: {.lede}
The list of characters is **open-ended**: Unicode defines well over a hundred thousand. The list of bytes is **closed**: 256 values.
:::

```text
çay   2 tokens  [b'\xc3\xa7', b'ay']
şişe  3 tokens  [b'\xc5\x9fi', b'\xc5\x9f', b'e']
ŞİŞE  6 tokens  [b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'\xc4\xb0', b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'E']
😀     2 tokens  [b'\xf0\x9f\x98', b'\x80']
```

- A tokenizer that starts from bytes has a complete alphabet from the first step: [nothing becomes `<UNK>`, rare characters just become expensive]{.hl}
- `ç` is one token: its two bytes were frequent enough to merge. `ŞİŞE` costs twice what `şişe` does
- The merges are not bound to character boundaries: `b'\xc5'` is *half a character*

::: {.src}
`cl100k_base` · Radford et al. 2019 · Gage 1994
:::

::: {.notes}
A tokenizer that starts from characters has an alphabet made of the characters
in its training text. However much text it sees, some character can still be
missing. A tokenizer that starts from bytes cannot meet a symbol it does not
know; every text in every language is a sequence of the 256 values.

The output is from OpenAI's byte-level `cl100k_base`. Read three things in it:
`ç` is a single token; capital `Ş` was rare in training, so its two bytes never
merged; the emoji is split the same way. A token can hold a whole character,
several characters, or only part of one.

A short note on history: the name BPE comes from a data-compression algorithm
published in 1994 (Gage 1994). GPT-2 introduced byte-level BPE with a
50,257-token vocabulary (Radford et al. 2019).

Keep two questions apart. A byte-level design guarantees *coverage*. How *many*
tokens a language costs is a separate question: it depends on how much of that
language the tokenizer's training data held. The measurement for Turkish comes
in a moment.

BPE is not the only way to learn a subword vocabulary. It has two relatives:
WordPiece, which BERT uses, and Unigram, which T5 uses. The book explains them
in Chapter 8, where it looks at BERT's tokenizer; Chapter 2 keeps a collapsed
deep-dive box for the curious. This lecture uses BPE alone.
:::

## Byte fallback: spelling an unknown character out in bytes

::: {.lede}
A third design: the vocabulary is built from characters, but one token for each of the 256 byte values is added to it.
:::

```text
byte_fallback=False  vocabulary  20  ['▁', 'ç', 'a', 'y']  ->  ' ⁇ ay'
byte_fallback=True   vocabulary 276  ['▁', '<0xC3>', '<0xA7>', 'a', 'y']  ->  'çay'
```

- SentencePiece was trained twice on eight Turkish words with no `ç` in them; both models were then given `çay`
- Off: `ç` gets the "unknown" id, and turned back into text [the letter is gone]{.con} (`⁇`)
- On: the two bytes of `ç` are written instead (C3 is 195, A7 is 167), and [`çay` comes back intact]{.pro}

::: {.src}
`sentencepiece` 0.2.2, `byte_fallback=True`
:::

::: {.notes}
The tokenizer handles the characters it knows as usual. When it meets one it
does not know, it writes that character's UTF-8 bytes one by one with the byte
tokens instead of writing `<UNK>`.

Tie the numbers to the previous slide: `<0xC3>` and `<0xA7>` are the two bytes
from the `çay` table (195 and 167). The vocabulary grew from 20 to 276: the 256
byte tokens were added.

The leading `▁` marks where a word starts; it comes back a few slides on.

The code for the experiment is in the chapter; fifteen lines.
:::

## Who pays for Turkish

::: {.lede}
Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, official English and Turkish texts, through OpenAI's tokenizers:
:::

::: {.roomy}
| Tokenizer | English | Turkish | Turkish costs |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `cl100k_base` (GPT-3.5/4) | 170 chars → 33 tokens · 5.15 chars/token | 160 chars → 60 tokens · 2.67 chars/token | **1.82×** more tokens |
| `o200k_base` | 170 chars → 33 tokens · 5.15 chars/token | 160 chars → 46 tokens · 3.48 chars/token | **1.39×** more tokens |
:::

::: {.takeaway}
APIs bill per token and context windows are measured in tokens: [a Turkish speaker pays more money for less context.]{.hl} Newer tokenizers narrow the gap; they do not close it.
:::

::: {.src}
Petrov et al. 2023
:::

::: {.notes}
Now the part that matters if you work in a language other than English. A
tokenizer is trained on a corpus, and how efficiently it encodes a language
depends on how much of that language the corpus contained — which, for the
tokenizers most people use, means mostly English.

Same sentence, same meaning, 1.82× the tokens on the GPT-3.5/4 tokenizer; 1.39×
with `o200k_base`. This is a documented and measured unfairness across
languages (Petrov et al. 2023), not a rounding error.

The measurement is a short `tiktoken` script in the chapter; students rerun it
on their own text in Exercise 1.
:::

## What a Turkish word costs

| Word | What the tokenizer sees | Tokens |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `ev` | `' ev'` | 1 |
| `evler` | `' ev'` `ler` | 2 |
| `evlerimiz` | `' ev'` `ler` `im` `iz` | 4 |
| `evlerimizden` | `' ev'` `ler` `im` `iz` `den` | **5** |

- *from our houses*: three English words, three tokens. [Better linguistics, worse bill.]{.hl}
- The splits match the real morphology at three of four boundaries. The asterisk is `im|iz`: *-imiz* ("our") is a single morpheme

::: {.takeaway}
Bring Turkish text into one form before it reaches the tokenizer: `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)`
:::

::: {.notes}
Why does it happen? Turkish is agglutinative: meaning is built by stacking
suffixes onto a stem (Oflazer 1994). English builds meaning with separate words,
which is exactly what a frequency-based merge algorithm captures well.

The good news, with one honest asterisk. `ev|ler|im|iz|den` lines up with the
real morphology at three of its four boundaries — *ev* (house), *-ler*
(plural), *-den* (from) — and nobody supplied a rule of Turkish grammar. The
asterisk is `im|iz`: *-imiz* ("our") is a single morpheme that BPE cut in half,
because `im` and `iz` are each frequent on their own. Frequency is a good proxy
for morphology, not a substitute. The newer `o200k_base` cuts the same word as
`ev|ler|imiz|den`, so where the cut falls depends on the merge table, not on
the language.

One sentence is enough for the NFC line in the takeaway: a letter with a mark,
such as `ö`, can be stored in two different ways (one code point, or `o` plus a
separate "two dots" mark). The two look the same on screen, but a tokenizer
counts them differently. Every measurement in the chapter was taken after that
call.

Point at the space in front of `' ev'` in the table; it is the subject of the
next slide.
:::

## Where did the spaces go? {.smaller}

`evlerimizden geldik` ("we came from our houses") — the same two words in three tokenizer families (`␣` stands for a space):

| Family (tokenizer that was run) | Tokens | How it marks the word boundary |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **GPT** (`cl100k_base`) | `ev` `ler` `im` `iz` `den` `␣geld` `ik` | Glues the space onto the first token of the *next* word |
| **SentencePiece** (XLM-R) | `▁ev` `lerimiz` `den` `▁geldi` `k` | Puts a visible `▁` at the start of a word |
| **WordPiece** (multilingual BERT) | `ev` `##leri` `##mi` `##zde` `##n` `geldi` `##k` | Puts `##` in front of every piece that *continues* a word |

- **Words first, then pieces.** The text is first cut into words at whitespace and punctuation: **pre-tokenization**. [No token ever spans two words]{.hl}
- To turn tokens back into text, where a word starts is written on the token itself
- SentencePiece does not pre-tokenize: it treats the space as an ordinary character and replaces it with `▁`

::: {.src}
Kudo & Richardson 2018
:::

::: {.notes}
Why does the `' ev'` token on the previous slide carry a space in front? This
slide is the answer.

GPT's BPE tokenizers and BERT's WordPiece do not apply their merges to the
sentence as a whole. They first cut the text into words (GPT-2 does it with a
regular expression) and only then split each word into subwords, inside its own
boundaries.

Cutting the text into words throws the spaces away. Ask the class: how would
you join the pieces `ev`, `ler`, `geld`, `ik` — as `evler geldik`, or as
`ev ler geld ik`? The only way to know is to write on the token where a word
starts. The three families do it with three different marks, and all three
carry the same information: "a new word starts here".

That SentencePiece does not pre-tokenize is what makes it work for languages
such as Japanese and Chinese, which do not put spaces between words.

All three rows of the table were produced by running the tokenizers.
:::

## The four stages of a tokenizer {.smaller}

`Çay içtik, sonra evlerimizden çıktık.` ("We drank tea, then we left our houses.") — step by step through multilingual BERT's tokenizer:

| Stage | Output |
|:--|:--|
| **1. Normalization** | `cay ictik, sonra evlerimizden cıktık.` |
| **2. Pre-tokenization** | `cay` `ictik` `,` `sonra` `evlerimizden` `cıktık` `.` |
| **3. Subword encoding** | `cay` `ic` `##tik` `,` `sonra` `ev` `##leri` `##mi` `##zde` `##n` `cıktı` `##k` `.` |
| **4. Special tokens** | `[CLS]` `cay` `ic` `##tik` `,` `sonra` `ev` `##leri` `##mi` `##zde` `##n` `cıktı` `##k` `.` `[SEP]` |

- What the first stage deletes does not come back: the model [can no longer tell `çay` (tea) from `cay`]{.con}
- Subword encoding runs *inside* each word: `evlerimizden` is five pieces, `sonra` stays whole
- What reaches the model is not these pieces but their ids: `101, 21373, 11797, …, 119, 102`

::: {.src}
`bert-base-multilingual-uncased`, `tokenizers` 0.22
:::

::: {.notes}
Text goes through four stages, in order, before it reaches the model. This
slide follows them on one Turkish sentence; every row of the table is real
output.

Normalization: this tokenizer lowercases everything and strips the marks from
letters. `Çay` → `cay`, `içtik` → `ictik`. `ı` survived because Unicode defines
it as a letter of its own, not as an `i` with a mark added.

Pre-tokenization: the comma and the full stop became pieces of their own.

Special tokens: `[CLS]` at the start of the sequence, `[SEP]` at the end.

Tokenizers do not all fill these four stages the same way. The case-sensitive
version of the same model (`bert-base-multilingual-cased`) leaves the text
untouched in the first stage. GPT's byte-level tokenizers do no normalization
at all. SentencePiece skips pre-tokenization.
:::

## Special tokens

| token | what it is for |
|:--|:--|
| `[UNK]` | input with no vocabulary entry; nearly absent at byte level |
| `[PAD]` | padding that evens up short sequences in a batch; the attention mask ignores it |
| `[CLS]` | in the BERT family, the leading token whose vector stands for the whole sequence |
| `[SEP]` | the boundary between two segments, a question and a passage for instance |
| BOS / EOS | start and end of sequence; in generative models EOS is how the model says it is finished |

::: {.takeaway}
The spellings differ by model — `<s>`, `</s>`, `<|endoftext|>` do these jobs. [Special tokens take their share of the context window too.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide closes a question students often ask: "what are those
square-bracket things in the tokenizer output?"

The `[CLS]` and `[SEP]` on the previous slide are what the fourth stage adds.
Count them when you count tokens; they take their share of the window.
:::

## Intuition check · characters {.question}

::: {.ask}
A character vocabulary is tiny, needs no training, and in bytes never meets an unknown symbol. Why does everyone use subwords?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Sequence length is the binding constraint**
- Attention grows with the *square* of sequence length, everything else in the layer linearly (Ch. 7)
- A sequence 5× longer costs between 5× and 25×, depending on where you sit relative to the model width — and the quadratic term eventually wins
- [Subword tokenization is a representation trade-off: you buy shorter sequences by spending vocabulary]{.hl} — BPE really was a compression algorithm in 1994, but the goal here is choosing units
:::

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute before revealing (one click).

A character vocabulary is about 100 symbols for English, 256 if you work in
bytes. It has no out-of-vocabulary problem once the character set is closed —
which bytes guarantee and a hand-picked alphabet does not — and it needs no
training.

The tokenizer is the knob that trades vocabulary size against sequence length,
and BPE sets that knob using the statistics of the data rather than a human's
guess. The quadratic cost is Chapter 7's (Transformers and Attention).
:::

## Three granularities, side by side {.smaller}

| | Characters | Subwords (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram) | Whole words |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Vocabulary size** | [~100 for ASCII; 256 in bytes]{.pro} | 30k–100k | [Unbounded — it never closes]{.con} |
| **Out-of-vocabulary** | [Cannot arise if the character set is closed — guaranteed only in bytes]{.pro} | [Rare — cut into shorter pieces, provided the vocabulary covers every character or has a byte fallback]{.pro} | [Constant, and worst for the words you care about]{.con} |
| **Sequence length** | [5–10× longer: slower and more expensive]{.con} | [Moderate]{.pro} | [Shortest]{.pro} |
| **Meaning per unit** | [Almost none — `p` means nothing]{.con} | Partial; often morpheme-like | [A whole unit of meaning]{.pro} |
| **Morphologically rich languages** | Handles them, expensively | [Well — it recovered Turkish suffixes]{.pro} | [Fails badly]{.con} |
| **Needs training** | [No]{.pro} | [Yes, on a corpus]{.con} | [No]{.pro} |

::: {.takeaway}
Subwords win because [they are the only column without a fatal entry.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Every tokenizer students will ever meet sits somewhere on this line, and the
whole design problem is that the two ends fail in opposite directions.

Two details from the chapter's full table. Character vocabularies run to tens of
thousands for multilingual Unicode — 256 only if you work in bytes. And the
subword out-of-vocabulary entry has a condition: WordPiece, which cannot spell
an unknown character out in bytes, still emits `[UNK]`.

The WordPiece and Unigram in the column heading are BPE's two relatives. The
book explains how the three differ in Chapter 8, where it looks at BERT's
tokenizer.

That is usually how engineering compromises win — not by being best at
anything, but by having no weakness bad enough to rule them out.
:::

:::

::: {.column .compact width="45%"}
- 20 Newsgroups: 11,314 documents, 2.29M tokens, 78,649 distinct types
- Top 10 types → 20.99% of all tokens; top 1,000 → 71.04%; top 10,000 → 92.50%
- [Half the vocabulary appears exactly once]{.hl}: 49.0% of the types, 1.69% of the tokens
- $f(r) \propto r^{-\alpha}$ — close to a straight line on log-log axes. Take it as a *shape*, not a fitted model
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Lang 1995 · Zipf 1949
:::

::: {.notes}
Open with the question the chapter opens with. Read a million words of your own
domain and keep every distinct one. How many do you get? And more usefully — if
you then read a second million, how many *new* ones appear? The answer to that
second question is what makes tokenization hard.

The plot is a static copy of the chapter's interactive one: 50 log-spaced sample
ranks, dots, with a dashed line for a clean α = 1 through the top word. In the
book students can switch to linear axes: the distribution then looks like a
single spike and a flat line, and the flat line is where almost all of the
vocabulary lives.

The single-occurrence words are *hapax legomena*: 49% of everything you would
have to store, and 1.7% of what you would ever see. Top 100 types → 46.99%.

"Close to" is doing work. The tenth-ranked word appears 26,985 times, not the
roughly 10,600 a clean α = 1 would predict — the head of the distribution is
flatter than the law, which is what Mandelbrot's correction
f(r) ∝ (r + b)^(−α) exists to absorb.
:::

## If you need the exponent, do not fit it with a regression

::: {.lede}
Least squares on a log-log rank-frequency plot is the standard way to get a wrong power-law exponent — for three separate reasons:
:::

1. Ranking is a transform of the data, so rank and frequency are **mechanically correlated**
2. The log transform makes the errors **heteroscedastic**, which breaks the OLS assumption
3. Every point in the long, noisy tail **counts as much as** the well-estimated head

::: {.takeaway}
The published fix: maximum likelihood with a fitted lower cutoff $x_{\min}$, plus a Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit test — [not an $R^2$.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.src}
Clauset et al. 2009
:::

::: {.notes}
Nothing in this chapter depends on the exact value of the exponent; the shape
is the lesson.
:::

## Heaps' law: the vocabulary never closes

- Zipf describes the corpus you already have. *How many new words does the next million bring?* needs a second law
- Count distinct types as you walk through the corpus: $|V| \approx K N^{\beta}$, with $\beta$ typically between 0.4 and 0.6
- The exponent is below 1, yet $\mathrm{d}|V|/\mathrm{d}N = K\beta N^{\beta-1}$ is strictly positive for every $N$ while shrinking towards zero
- [It looks flat on a plot long before it stops growing]{.hl} — that is the trap

::: {.takeaway}
On realistic corpora you keep meeting new types as the data grows; there is only a size at which you stop meeting them *quickly*. Heaps is an empirical relationship that models it.
:::

::: {.src}
Heaps 1978
:::

::: {.notes}
Three consequences follow from Zipf and Heaps, and they shaped everything in
modern NLP:

1. A word-level vocabulary can never be complete. New words arrive forever —
   names, part numbers, typos, compounds. This is the argument for subwords, in
   one sentence.
2. Most of the vocabulary is statistically useless. A word seen once supports
   no estimate of anything. This is why `min_df` exists, and why it cuts the
   matrix far more than stop word removal does: it deletes most of your columns
   while deleting very little of your text.
3. Frequency and informativeness are almost opposites. The words you see most
   tell you least. That observation is the seed of TF-IDF.

The chapter shows the ten-line loop that counts distinct types every 10,000
tokens.
:::

## Always look at your top-50 list

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="36%"}
::: {.stat}
[62,043]{.bignum}

occurrences of `'ax` — the **second** most frequent token, ahead of *to*, *a* and *of*
:::
:::

::: {.column width="64%"}
- Not a word: it comes from 13 of 11,314 documents — one quoted copy of a corrupted binary posting, and twelve replies that quoted it back
- The largest single document contributes 11,147 of the 62,043
- Term frequency: the second most important word in English. Document frequency: 0.1% of documents
- The leading apostrophe is *ours* — our regex `[a-z']+`; the default `token_pattern` gives `ax`
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
The gap between [“appears often” and “appears in many places”]{.hl} is exactly what the next section is built on.
:::

::: {.notes}
A real bug that has been sitting in a famous benchmark dataset for thirty years.

The apostrophe nuance sharpens the point rather than weakening it: our regex
treats `'` as a word character, so the corpus junk and our own tokenizer choice
combine into this particular string. The artefact is in the data, but its shape
is a preprocessing decision — which is the lesson of the whole section.

The habit, in the chapter's words: always look at your top-50 list.
:::

## From string to vector: six steps

::: {.lede}
Four maintenance logs — d1 `the pump failed` · d2 `the pump was replaced` · d3 `the valve failed` · d4 `the seal leak was repaired`
:::

| Step | For d1 = `the pump failed` | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Tokenize | `the` · `pump` · `failed` | string → units |
| **1** · Index | `failed`→0, `pump`→2, `the`→6 | every distinct token gets an address |
| **2** · One-hot | `pump` = `[0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]` | a word as a vector |
| **3** · Sum = counts | `[1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]` | word order is gone |
| **4** · [TF-IDF weights]{.hl} | `[1.51 0 1.51 … 1.00 …]` | rare words weigh more |
| **5** · [L2 normalize]{.hl} | `[0.64 0 0.64 … 0.42 …]` | document length is gone |
| **6** · Compare | cos(d1, d3) = 0.528 | search, clustering, classification read only this |

::: {.notes}
The core of the chapter: four short maintenance logs taken all the way from
strings to vectors you can compute distances on, skipping no step and showing
every intermediate number.

This table is the chapter's pipeline figure. Every number is the one the code
actually produces for d1. The vocabulary index is alphabetical, so `failed` is
column 0, `pump` column 2 and `the` column 6.

The two highlighted steps are the only places where any *statistics* happen —
everything else is bookkeeping.
:::

## Steps 1–2 · an index, then a one-hot vector

```text
['failed' 'leak' 'pump' 'repaired' 'replaced' 'seal' 'the' 'valve' 'was']
```

- Nine words: every vector from here on lives in $\mathbb{R}^9$. A real corpus has 30,000–500,000

```text
pump  : [0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]
valve : [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0]
        ------------------- multiply position by position
        [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0]  -> sum = 0
```

- [Every word is orthogonal to every other word]{.hl}: `pump` is exactly as similar to `valve` as to `repaired`
- A filing system, not a meaning system. Fixing that is the whole of Ch. 3

::: {.notes}
Step 1 has no meaning in it. Collect every distinct token, sort, assign each an
integer — the word's *address*. `CountVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus)` then
`get_feature_names_out()` prints the line on the slide.

Step 2. An index is not a vector: we cannot do arithmetic on a filing-cabinet
drawer number. The simplest encoding of a single word is a vector of zeros with
a single 1 at the word's address.

It is a legitimate vector and almost useless on its own. The dot product of
*any* two distinct one-hot vectors is zero — the single 1 in one always lands on
a 0 in the other. The representation contains no notion of similarity at all,
only identity: the vector for `pump` says *where the word is kept*, and nothing
about what it is like.

Tell students to hold onto that sentence: fixing it is the entire subject of
Chapter 3 (Embeddings).
:::

## Step 3 · a document is the sum of its one-hots

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
- Add up the one-hot vectors of every token in a document: a **count vector**
- That is **bag-of-words** — the multiset of tokens, order discarded
- Do it for all four documents: [the document-term matrix]{.hl}, the central object of classical NLP
- A statistician's **design matrix**: documents are observations, words are features
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```text
          d1  d2  d3  d4
failed     1   0   1   0
leak       0   0   0   1
pump       1   1   0   0
repaired   0   0   0   1
replaced   0   1   0   0
seal       0   0   0   1
the        1   1   1   1
valve      0   0   1   0
was        0   1   0   1
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
One word, one vector. But we set out to compare *documents*, and a document is
many words at once. The simplest possible answer works: add them up.

`d1 tokens: ['the', 'pump', 'failed']` → `d1 vector: [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]`.

The matrix is shown transposed so it fits — it is 4 documents × 9 terms; rows
are documents, columns are words.

A *feature* is one measured column of your data — here, one word. For
statisticians it is simply a predictor variable under a different name, and
everything they know about regression with many correlated, mostly-zero
predictors now applies.
:::

## Step 4 · counts are the wrong numbers

::: {.lede}
`the` is in all four documents and distinguishes nothing; `valve` alone makes d3 distinctive. Raw counts treat them the same.
:::

$$\mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1 + n}{1 + \mathrm{df}(t)}\right) + 1$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .compact width="47%"}
- $n = 4$. `pump` is in 2 documents: $\ln\frac{5}{3} + 1 = 1.511$
- `the` is in all 4: $\ln\frac{5}{5} + 1 = 1$ — [down-weighted, not deleted]{.hl}
- The $1+$ terms act as one extra document containing every term once
:::

::: {.column width="53%"}
| On 20 Newsgroups | df | df/N | idf |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| `the` | 9,477 | 0.838 | 1.18 |
| `is` | 7,034 | 0.622 | 1.48 |
| `car` | 394 | 0.035 | 4.35 |
| `encryption` | 169 | 0.015 | 5.20 |
| `gravitational` | 8 | 0.001 | 8.14 |
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Spärck Jones 1972
:::

::: {.notes}
We want a weight that is high when a word is frequent *in this document* and
rare *across documents*. Splitting that into two factors gives TF-IDF.

Term frequency is the *raw* count. scikit-learn does not divide by document
length here, because the L2 normalisation in step 5 handles length. Many
textbooks define tf = c(t,d)/|d|, or 1 + log c(t,d), and the numbers differ. In
SMART notation — tf × idf × normalisation — scikit-learn's default is roughly
`ntc` (natural tf, smoothed idf, cosine normalisation); the classic IR default
is `ltc`, with logarithmic tf. `sublinear_tf=True` moves you from n to l.

Document frequency df(t) is how many documents contain the word at all. We want
the weight to fall as df rises, so we invert it; raw inversion is too
aggressive, so we take a logarithm (Spärck Jones 1972).

Reading the formula: the imaginary extra document is why df can never be zero
and no weight can run away — the same add-one idea as Laplace smoothing in
Chapter 6. The trailing +1 guarantees a word appearing everywhere still gets
weight 1 rather than 0. This is scikit-learn's exact formula; other libraries
differ in the details — a classic source of "why don't my numbers match".

Worked: ln(1.667) + 1 = 0.511 + 1 = 1.511. For `the` the ratio collapses to 1,
the log to 0, and the term is left standing on the floor weight of 1: it gets
one vote while `pump` gets one and a half. On the toy corpus, every word unique
to one document gets 1.9163, and the manual values match `idf_` with a maximum
absolute difference of 0.0.

The librarian's version: ask for "the book about pumps" — *the* narrows the
shelf not at all, *pumps* narrows it to a metre of shelving. IDF is a number for
how much a word narrows the search.

The book's IDF widget: the curve is flat above ~20% of documents — once a word
is common, getting commoner barely changes anything. All the action is in the
first few percent, which is where content words live.
:::

## Intuition check · the logarithm {.question}

::: {.ask}
Why does IDF use a logarithm?
:::

::: {.fragment}
The weak answer: *"to prevent the weight from getting too big."*
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Diminishing returns** — 1 vs 10 documents out of 10,000 is a big difference in specificity; 5,000 vs 5,010 is none
- **A probability in disguise** — $\log \frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)} = -\log P(t)$, the *self-information* of seeing the term
- **Zipf closes the loop** — on a scale that skewed, the log measures a difference as a *ratio*, as with income or city size
- Spärck Jones proposed IDF on empirical grounds in 1972; [the theory was reverse-engineered later]{.hl}
:::

::: {.src}
Spärck Jones 1972 · Robertson 2004
:::

::: {.notes}
Two clicks: the weak answer, then the better one. This is one of the most common
interview questions in the whole field.

Diminishing returns: informativeness is not linear in rarity. The log compresses
the top of the range and preserves resolution at the bottom, which matches how
specificity actually behaves.

Probability: if df(t)/n estimates the probability that a random document
contains t, then log(n/df) = −log P(t). Rare events carry more information; the
log is not a trick for making numbers smaller, it is what information *is*.
Robertson (2004) is the careful treatment.

Zipf: a handful of words have enormous counts and tens of thousands have tiny
ones. On a scale that skewed raw differences mislead; the log straightens the
distribution into a line — the same reason you log-transform income or city
size, where a few giants flatten everyone else off the scale.
:::

## Step 5 · multiply, then normalize

```text
counts        : [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]
times idf     : [1.5108 0. 1.5108 0. 0. 0. 1. 0. 0.]
l2 norm       : 2.3591
normalized    : [0.6404 0. 0.6404 0. 0. 0. 0.4239 0. 0.]
sklearn row d1: [0.6404 0. 0.6404 0. 0. 0. 0.4239 0. 0.]
```

$$\lVert v \rVert_2 = \sqrt{1.5108^2 + 1.5108^2 + 1.0000^2} \approx 2.3591 \qquad \tfrac{1.5108}{2.3591} = 0.6404 \qquad \tfrac{1.0000}{2.3591} = 0.4239$$

- The hand computation and `TfidfVectorizer` agree to every digit: there is no magic in the library
- [L2 normalization is not cosmetic]{.hl}: without it a long document has a large vector simply for being long
- On the unit sphere only *direction* — the mix of words — carries information

::: {.notes}
TF-IDF is the product, computed cell by cell. d1 has three non-zero positions,
each with a count of 1: 1.5108 for `failed`, 1.5108 for `pump`, 1.0000 for `the`.
The length is the ordinary Pythagorean one extended to nine dimensions — square,
add, take the root: √(2.28259 + 2.28259 + 1.00000) = √5.56518 ≈ 2.3591.
Intermediate values are rounded for display; at full precision the norm is
2.35906509…, which is what the library uses.

The six zero entries contribute nothing, which is why this stays cheap even with
200,000 columns.

Without normalization every similarity comparison becomes a comparison of
document lengths. Think of every document on a sphere of the same radius: a
50-word and a 5,000-word report both end at unit *length* — the squares of the
components sum to one, not the components.

One document cannot be put on the sphere: an empty one, or one whose every word
is out of vocabulary. Its norm is 0 and cosine with it is 0/0. scikit-learn
returns a zero row and a cosine of 0 — a convention rather than an answer; count
such documents before trusting any similarity built on them.

This combination is not the only one anyone tried: Salton & Buckley (1988)
compared a large family of weighting schemes empirically, and this is roughly
the one that won.

The book's matrix widget: under TF-IDF the `the` column fades to the lightest
non-zero weight in each row, while `valve` — unique to d3 — becomes the darkest
cell in the matrix.
:::

## Step 6 · cosine similarity

$$\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert} = \sum_{i} a_i b_i \quad \text{(when both are unit length)}$$

$$\cos(\text{d1}, \text{d3}) = \underbrace{0.6404 \times 0.5729}_{\texttt{failed}} + \underbrace{0.4239 \times 0.3792}_{\texttt{the}} = 0.3669 + 0.1607 = 0.528$$

- `failed` supplies 70% of the similarity and `the` 30% — though each occurs exactly once in each document
- [The weighting is what decides which shared word counts as evidence]{.hl}
- d1 and d4 share only `the`: cosine 0.26 under raw counts, 0.11 under TF-IDF
- A cosine is the cosine of an angle — not a calibrated "26% similar"

::: {.notes}
Every document is now a point in R⁹, which finally lets us ask: are these two
documents about the same thing? 1 means identical direction, 0 means no shared
vocabulary.

Only positions where *both* vectors are non-zero can contribute, so the
nine-dimensional sum has exactly two live terms. Under raw counts the two shared
words would have contributed equally.

Full matrices from the chapter, TF-IDF then raw counts:

- d1–d2 0.458 (raw 0.577); d1–d3 0.528 (0.667); d1–d4 0.112 (0.258)
- d2–d3 0.125 (0.289); d2–d4 0.286 (0.447); d3–d4 0.100 (0.258)

Every pair drops, and the pairs that drop most are the ones whose only common
ground was a stop word.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
On unit vectors $\lVert a - b \rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos(a,b)$: here $2 - 2(0.651) = 0.698$, a distance of 0.836. [Euclid and cosine now rank every pair the same — provided you normalized first.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Because Euclidean distance is dominated by document length. A 50-word incident
report and a 5,000-word one about the identical failure differ enormously in
vector *magnitude* and hardly at all in *direction*. Cosine asks "what is this
document about?" rather than "how much of it is there?"

The figure: A and B are the same report at two lengths, on a single ray — yet
Euclidean distance puts A more than six times closer to C, which is about
something else entirely. After L2 normalization A and B become the same point,
and only the angle is left to measure.

Where 2 − 2cos comes from, two lines worth doing once:
‖a − b‖² = (a − b)·(a − b) = a·a − 2(a·b) + b·b. On unit vectors a·a = b·b = 1
and a·b *is* the cosine, so ‖a − b‖² = 1 − 2cos + 1 = 2 − 2cos.

Distance is a strictly decreasing function of similarity: as the cosine climbs
from 0 to 1, the squared distance falls from 2 to 0. So nearest-neighbour search
under Euclidean distance and under cosine return the same ranked list — provided
the vectors were normalized. Skip normalization and a retrieval index built on
L2 distance quietly starts ranking by document length instead of topic. The
identity comes back in Chapter 3 whenever someone swaps a cosine index for an L2
index. It is the answer interviewers are usually fishing for.
:::

## What bag-of-words cannot do

| It cannot represent | Two documents | Under bag-of-words |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Word order** | *the pump failed and the valve is fine* / *the valve failed and the pump is fine* | the same point: identical vectors, cosine 1.0 |
| **Scope of negation** | *no leak was found* / *a leak was found* | cosine 0.866 (counts), 0.777 (TF-IDF) — 100% if *no* is a stop word |
| **Synonymy** | *pump failed* / *pump broke* | share nothing beyond `pump` |
| **Polysemy** | `Apple` the company / `apple` the fruit | the same column |

::: {.takeaway}
Bigrams buy back a little (cosine 0.714 on the first pair), but on a real corpus they took the features from 32,318 to 249,522 — [and made accuracy worse.]{.hl} A local patch; the real fix is Ch. 7.
:::

::: {.notes}
The limits are severe enough that the rest of the book exists to fix them.

Word order: not "represents it poorly" — cannot represent it at all. Two reports
naming opposite pieces of failed equipment are the same point in space. No
classifier, however good, can separate them, because the information was
destroyed before the classifier saw it. With bigrams the vocabulary goes from 7
to 9 and the pair becomes distinguishable; on a real corpus the vocabulary
explodes (7.7×). The real fix is Chapter 7 (Transformers and Attention).

Negation: the word *not* is a feature like any other, and a classifier can learn
that its presence shifts the odds — what a bag of words cannot recover is *what*
was negated. The default `token_pattern` drops the one-letter "a", so the
vocabulary is found, leak, no, was. TF-IDF helps a little, nowhere near enough.
Most default stop word lists contain *no*. This is the single most common way a
text classifier silently fails a safety-critical review — it costs real money
in production.

Synonymy and polysemy: every word is its own island, exactly as with one-hot
vectors in Step 2 — the problem Chapter 3 solves.
:::

## Does any of this still matter?

::: {.lede}
A real experiment: four newsgroups, 2,327 training and 1,550 test documents, logistic regression, nothing tuned.
:::

::: {.roomy}
| Setup | Accuracy | Features |
|:--|--:|--:|
| raw counts | 0.767 | 32,318 |
| counts + stop words | 0.795 | 32,014 |
| tf-idf | 0.831 | 32,318 |
| tf-idf + stop words | **0.853** | 32,014 |
| tf-idf + bigrams | 0.819 | 249,522 |
| tf-idf + sublinear tf | 0.843 | 32,318 |
:::

::: {.notes}
Yes — and students should be able to say why with numbers rather than opinion.

The categories are sci.med, sci.space, rec.autos and talk.politics.guns, with
headers, footers and quotes removed. Each setup is a scikit-learn pipeline of a
vectorizer and `LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)`. The results are
deterministic: the default lbfgs solver takes no randomness. The full code is
in the chapter; Exercise 4 reproduces it.

Ask the room to read the six lines before the next slide: what would you
conclude?
:::

## Four lessons — and how far to trust them

1. **TF-IDF is worth 6.4 accuracy points** over raw counts — no extra data, no tuning
2. **Stop word removal helps here** (+2.2) — on topic classification; it would hurt sentiment or negation detection
3. **Bigrams made it worse** while multiplying the features by 7.7: more features is more variance
4. **`sublinear_tf` points the same way** (0.843 vs 0.831): $1 + \log(\text{tf})$ — diminishing returns on the term-frequency side

::: {.takeaway}
Point estimates, no intervals: near 0.83 on 1,550 documents, roughly ±1.9 points — and lessons 3 and 4 rest on a gap of 1.2. [Read 1–2 as findings, 3–4 as directions.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The weighting is not decoration. There is no universal answer on stop words.

scikit-learn's own documentation calls `stop_words='english'` problematic: it is
not a general-purpose list, its selection criteria are undocumented, and a few
entries can never be produced by the default `token_pattern`. If stop words
matter to a result, write the list yourself and print it.

On the caution — the book asks the same of everyone else. The six models see
the identical test documents, so the right instrument is a *paired* test such as
McNemar's (McNemar 1947), which has far more power than comparing two
independent intervals. The chapter did not run one. When it is your experiment,
run the paired test and report it.

One more warning about generalising from six lines. Every number here comes from
English topic classification on long documents, and two of the four lessons
reverse when the task changes. On Turkish product reviews — short documents,
sentiment rather than topic — Chapter 4 measures the opposite on both counts:
bigrams give the largest single gain in that chapter, and plain counting beats
TF-IDF, because IDF down-weights exactly the frequent sentiment words that carry
the signal. The transferable lesson is the method, not the ranking.
:::

## Readable, and tiny

```text
rec.autos            car, cars, engine, ford, oil, dealer, drive, price
sci.med              msg, doctor, disease, medical, pain, patients, treatment
sci.space            space, nasa, orbit, moon, launch, earth, spacecraft
talk.politics.guns   gun, guns, weapons, fbi, law, government, firearms
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.stat}
[213×]{.bignum}

smaller as a sparse matrix: 2.8 MB instead of 601.6 MB
:::
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
- Ask the model what it learned and it tells you, in words. [No transformer will hand you that table]{.hl}
- 2,327 × 32,318, density 0.312% — 99.7% zeros
- Training takes seconds on a laptop; inference is a sparse dot product; no GPU anywhere
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The other reason to care is that the model is *readable*: the table is the top
features the TF-IDF-plus-logistic-regression model learned for each class. When
you have to defend a model to a safety board, a regulator or a sceptical plant
manager, this matters more than four points of accuracy.

The matrix stores 234,281 non-zeros. Dense float64 would need 601.6 MB; sparse
CSR actually needs 2.8 MB.

The chapter's summary table, "Bag-of-words, honestly", in one breath. Why it
survives: fast and tiny; legible; a strong baseline (0.853 here, and it beat
averaged embeddings in Chapter 3, then again on Turkish data in Chapter 4); no
training data beyond your own — nothing pretrained, nothing downloaded, no
vendor; deterministic and debuggable. Why it is not enough: no word order, no
synonymy (`car` and `automobile` are as unrelated as `car` and `banana`), no
polysemy (one column for `bank`), a vocabulary that never closes, and negation
with no scope.

The right reading is not "old technology, still surprisingly good". The two
columns describe *different tasks*. When the words that matter are literally
present and you need speed and an audit trail, this is the correct answer. When
meaning depends on order, context, or a word you did not anticipate, no amount
of tuning will save you.
:::

## Where this is actually deployed

- **Ticket triage at Uber** — COTA runs this chapter's pipeline almost line for line: TF-IDF, LSA, then cosine ranking. Resolution time down around 10%
- **Google's text classification guide** — TF-IDF n-grams are the most accurate of the encodings it compares; accuracy peaks around 20,000 features
- **Hybrid retrieval for RAG** — sparse BM25 catches the exact matches that embeddings blur: part numbers, error codes, surnames (Ch. 20)
- **Spam and abuse filtering** — cheap enough to run on every message, retrained in minutes; feature hashing avoids a vocabulary altogether
- **Near-duplicate detection** — Google's web-crawl deduplication runs on shingles and hashing, over billions of documents

::: {.src}
Uber Engineering 2018 · Google Developers 2022 · Weinberger et al. 2009 · Manku et al. 2007
:::

::: {.notes}
None of these are old history, and each is documented by the company that built
it.

Uber's COTA: clean, tokenize, remove stop words, lemmatize, TF-IDF, reduce with
LSA, then rank candidate solutions by cosine similarity to the ticket. The
write-up notes that the cosine-similarity ranker beat using the topic vectors
directly by 25% relative accuracy — because the raw vectors were too sparse.
That is this chapter's sparsity problem, in production, with a number attached.

Google's guide: beyond ~20,000 features, extra features contribute nothing and
eventually cause overfitting. Our bigram result — 249,522 features, worse
accuracy — is the same finding on a smaller corpus.

A *shingle* is a fixed-length window of words (or characters) slid across the
document; the windows overlap like roof tiles. The three-word shingles of *the
pump failed last night* are `the pump failed`, `pump failed last` and
`failed last night` — so shingles are exactly n-grams, the front half of this
chapter.

Search ranking gets its own slide next.
:::

## BM25 — and why both its knobs are already familiar {.smaller}

$$\mathrm{BM25}(q, d) = \sum_{t \in q} \mathrm{idf}(t) \cdot \frac{c(t,d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{c(t,d) + k_1\!\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|d|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)}$$

- Lucene — so Elasticsearch and OpenSearch — scores documents with BM25, a direct descendant of TF-IDF
- **$k_1$**: term frequency *saturates* towards $k_1 + 1$, so the tenth occurrence adds almost nothing — `sublinear_tf` with a tunable ceiling
- **$b \in [0,1]$**: from ignoring length ($b = 0$) to dividing by length relative to the average ($b = 1$) — the concern L2 addresses, with a dial instead of a switch
- Lucene's defaults: $k_1 = 1.2$, $b = 0.75$

::: {.takeaway}
[Always build the TF-IDF baseline first.]{.hl} If your transformer cannot beat it, you have learned something important about your data — cheaply.
:::

::: {.src}
Robertson & Zaragoza 2009
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the formula against what we just built. The idf factor is the same idea as
ours; BM25 uses a probabilistic variant. The fraction replaces raw term
frequency with a saturating one. And b handles the same *concern* L2
normalisation addresses — long documents should not win on length alone — with
a different formula.

If you have ever used a site search box, you have used this. Elastic's
"Practical BM25" blog series explains the formula and its two tuning constants
better than most textbooks.

The practical rule from the chapter: reach for TF-IDF when your labels are few,
your documents are long, your vocabulary is technical and exact-match matters,
or when you need a baseline by this afternoon.
:::

## Intuition check 1 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your TF-IDF matrix has 200,000 columns and 5,000 rows. Should you worry?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Not about memory: storage scales with the number of *non-zeros*, not rows × columns
- The real worry is statistical — 200,000 parameters from 5,000 observations: [a p ≫ n problem]{.hl}
- The usual answers: strong regularization (L2 or L1), and cutting features with `min_df`
- On the four-category corpus, `min_df=5` takes 32,318 columns to 6,281 — 81% gone
- Not free: the deleted columns still carry 11.6% of the token occurrences
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter's intuition checks: students answer before the reveal. If they can
answer all six, they understand the chapter better than the code implies.

Why is `min_df` so effective? The Zipf section already answered it: most of the
vocabulary occurs too rarely to support any estimate at all.

But what you throw away is not only the hapax legomena — it includes words a
reader actually meets. Whether the trade is worth it is an empirical question
rather than a rule; Exercise 4 asks students to measure it.
:::

## Intuition check 2 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Should IDF be computed on the training set, or on all your data?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **On the training set only**, then applied unchanged to test data
- IDF is a parameter estimated from data: computing it over train + test leaks the test distribution into your features
- In `scikit-learn`: `fit_transform` on train, `transform` on test — calling `fit_transform` twice is a real and common bug
- In production the IDF vector is [a model artifact you version and ship]{.hl}, not something recomputed per batch
:::

::: {.notes}
Otherwise your features drift silently as traffic changes.

This answer comes back in the first interview question at the end of the
lecture.
:::

## Intuition check 3 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
A word appears in every document. What is its TF-IDF weight?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- `scikit-learn`'s smoothed formula: $\mathrm{df} = n$ gives $\ln\frac{1+n}{1+n} + 1 = 1$ — it survives with weight 1, then L2 shrinks it relative to rarer terms
- The textbook unsmoothed $\log(n/\mathrm{df})$: exactly **0** — the term is deleted
- `smooth_idf=True` is the default
- [Knowing that the two conventions differ separates someone who has used the tool from someone who has read about it]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Connect back to Step 4: `the` landed exactly on the floor of 1.0 in our
four-document corpus.
:::

## Intuition check 4 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Why do we normalize document vectors, but not feature columns?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- The two normalizations answer different questions. L2 row normalization removes document *length*, so comparisons are about topic, not size
- Column standardization — subtracting each word's mean — would be a disaster: it destroys sparsity
- A column that is 99.7% zeros minus a non-zero mean: every zero becomes non-zero, and 2.8 MB becomes 601.6 MB
- [Sparsity is not an implementation detail; it dictates which operations you are allowed to perform]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The numbers are the ones from the "Readable, and tiny" slide: the 2,327 ×
32,318 matrix of the classification experiment.
:::

## Intuition check 5 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your search engine returns nothing for the part number “P-101”. Why?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```text
default    : ['101', '102', 'pump', 'tripped']
custom     : ['p-101', 'p-102', 'pump', 'tripped']
```

- Almost certainly the tokenizer: the default `token_pattern=r"(?u)\b\w\w+\b"` needs two or more word characters and does not cross the hyphen
- `P-101` silently became `101` — the same token as a page number, a quantity or a pressure reading
- Invisible: nothing errors, accuracy just sits lower. [Print `get_feature_names_out()` and actually read it]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
`P-102` also became a bare number. The two are still different tokens, but the
equipment prefix is gone.

In technical domains this class of bug is more damaging than any choice of
model. The habit that prevents it: after fitting any vectorizer, print the
feature names and read them. Actually read them. Exercise 2 practises exactly
this.
:::

## Intuition check 6 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
When is a bag-of-words model the *right* choice in 2026?
:::

::: {.fragment}
When at least two of these hold:

- very few labelled examples per class
- a domain-specific vocabulary where exact matching matters — part numbers, gene names, legal citations
- you must explain every prediction to someone with authority over you
- no GPU, or a hard latency budget
- long, topical documents rather than short, nuanced ones
:::

::: {.fragment}
And unconditionally: [as the baseline.]{.hl} "Our transformer gets 0.91" without "TF-IDF gets 0.89" has not measured anything.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two clicks: the conditions, then the unconditional answer.

The last sentence points to Chapter 22 (Evaluating LLM Systems).
:::

## Interview question 1 of 2 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your text classifier performs well offline and badly in production. Walk me through your debugging.
:::

::: {.fragment .compact}
A checklist, in cost order:

1. **Train/serve skew** — is the *identical* preprocessing running in both places, including the fitted `TfidfVectorizer` with its vocabulary and IDF vector?
2. **Vocabulary drift** — new product names and error codes map to no column at all
3. **Distribution shift** in the label mix
4. **A leak in the offline evaluation** — e.g. fitting the vectorizer *before* the train/test split
5. Only then, the model
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.takeaway}
[The fitted vectorizer is an output: save it, version it and ship it with the model weights.]{.hl}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Text representation is the most reliably examined topic in applied NLP
interviews, because it is where a candidate either has mental models or has
memorized library calls. The chapter has fourteen such questions; these two come
from its group "testing whether you have shipped something".

On attribution, from the chapter: pages headed "NLP questions asked at Google
and Amazon" are essentially all search-engine content with no evidence behind
the claim. The chapter's questions come from two credible free sources — Chip
Huyen's *Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews* and the *Machine Learning
Interviews* repository — neither of which ties individual questions to a named
company.

"Serving" is the stage after training, where the model answers real requests.
Once fitted, the vectorizer is no longer just code: it carries two things learned
from the training data. If production refits it instead of loading the same one,
the same sentence becomes two different vectors — and the model is innocent.

Saying that the fitted vectorizer must be saved, versioned and shipped alongside
the weights is the single answer that most distinguishes practitioners from
students.
:::

## Interview question 2 of 2 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Design a system to detect near-duplicate documents in a corpus of 100 million.
:::

::: {.fragment .compact}
$\binom{10^8}{2} \approx 5 \times 10^{15}$ pairs — 58 days at a billion comparisons a second. [Never enumerate the pairs.]{.hl}

1. **Shingling** — each document becomes a set of 5–9-word windows; duplicates care about order
2. **Jaccard** $|A \cap B| / |A \cup B|$ — defines "near-duplicate"
3. **MinHash** — a 128-number signature; two signatures agree at a position with probability equal to the Jaccard similarity
4. **LSH** — $b = 16$ bands of $r = 8$: threshold near 0.71; Jaccard 0.8 becomes a candidate 94.7% of the time, 0.3 only 0.1%
5. **Verify** — exact Jaccard on the candidate pairs only
:::

::: {.src}
Broder 1997 · Indyk & Motwani 1998
:::

::: {.notes}
They are testing one reflex: do not try to look at every pair. The answer cannot
be "make it faster" — it has to be "never enumerate the pairs". Each step fixes
the problem the previous one leaves behind.

1. Why shingles rather than bag-of-words: two documents using the same words in a
   different order are not duplicates, yet bag-of-words gives them the same
   vector.
2. Jaccard is the right measure; the problem is computing it — the sets are large
   and there are still 5 × 10¹⁵ pairs.
3. MinHash: compare 128 numbers instead of intersecting large sets; storage drops
   to a few hundred bytes per document. The pair count is still 5 × 10¹⁵.
4. LSH: split the signature into b bands of r rows (b × r = 128), hash each band
   into a bucket, and call two documents candidates only if they share a bucket in
   at least one band. That turns a quadratic problem into a near-linear one.
5. A manageable number of pairs, not billions.

This chapter's material is the *first* step, and it matters more than it looks:
did you case-fold, strip punctuation, use character windows instead of word
windows — each changes what counts as a duplicate.
:::

## Exercises (1 of 2)

::: {.compact}
1. **Tokenizer economics.** Take a paragraph of your own technical writing in Turkish and its English translation. Count tokens under two tokenizers (the Tokenizer Playground or `tiktoken`), compute the cost ratio, and estimate what it does to your annual API bill at 100,000 requests per month.
2. **Break the vectorizer.** Fit a `CountVectorizer` on ten documents from your own domain and print `get_feature_names_out()`. Find at least two wrong tokens — a destroyed identifier, a merged pair, a lost unit — fix them with `token_pattern`, and report what changed.
3. **Derive it by hand.** Compute the TF-IDF vector for d3 with pen and paper, then verify against `TfidfVectorizer`. If they disagree, is it the smoothing, the L2 normalisation, or the `token_pattern`?
4. **Replicate and extend.** Reproduce the classification table, then add TF-IDF with `min_df=5`. Does accuracy fall? How far did the feature count fall? Argue for one configuration to the colleague who has to maintain it.
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter's seven exercises, over two slides.

Exercise 3: if the hand computation and the library disagree, the disagreement
is almost always in one of those three places.
:::

## Exercises (2 of 2)

::: {.compact}
5. **Find the negation failure.** Construct two documents from your own field with opposite operational meaning and TF-IDF cosine similarity above 0.9. Then write the sentence you would put in a design review explaining why this model must not be used for that decision.
6. **Zipf on your own data.** Plot rank against frequency on log-log axes for a corpus you own. Does the line look straight? What are the top five tokens — is any of them an artifact like `'ax`?
7. **The interview exercise.** Work through the five-document TF-IDF ranking problem in §8.2.1 of Chip Huyen's book with pen and paper, including its follow-up: if one document mentions the query term three times instead of once, what happens to its rank, and is that desirable? Check yourself with `TfidfVectorizer`.
8. **Get the Turkish bill off a single sentence.** Collect 50–100 sentence pairs from a parallel text; for each language and tokenizer report the **median tokens per 1,000 characters** and its spread. Where in that spread does the single-sentence measurement land?
:::

::: {.notes}
Exercise 7's follow-up is really a question about term-frequency saturation —
exactly what BM25 adds and what `sublinear_tf` approximates. Link:
https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/contents/8.2.1-natural-language-processing.html
:::

| Source | By | Why |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [Let's build the GPT Tokenizer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE) · [minbpe](https://github.com/karpathy/minbpe) | Andrej Karpathy | BPE from scratch, Unicode included; if you do one thing, do this |
| [Speech and Language Processing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) | Jurafsky & Martin | Ch. 2 *Words and Tokens*, Ch. 5 *Embeddings* |
| [Introduction to Information Retrieval](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/irbook.html) | Manning, Raghavan & Schütze | The vector space model; its IDF page is the careful "why the logarithm" |
| [Hugging Face LLM Course, Ch. 6](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/1) | Hugging Face | Builds BPE, WordPiece and Unigram tokenizers |
| [The Tokenizer Playground](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Xenova/the-tokenizer-playground) | — | Try your name, your part numbers, a paragraph of Turkish |
| [scikit-learn: text feature extraction](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_extraction.html#text-feature-extraction) | scikit-learn | The exact smoothed TF-IDF used in this lecture |
| [Introduction to ML Interviews](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/) | Chip Huyen | Free; the most honest guide to what these interviews contain |

::: {.notes}
A selection from the chapter's list; the rest, for students who want more:

- Karpathy's video is two hours implementing BPE from scratch, including the
  Unicode handling the chapter measures on Turkish; minbpe is a few hundred lines
  of clean Python that build a GPT-grade tokenizer.
- 3Blue1Brown, *Large Language Models explained briefly*: seven minutes, the
  clearest short account of why text has to become numbers at all.
- Jurafsky & Martin: the chapters were renumbered in the January 2026 draft —
  older blog posts pointing at "Chapter 6 for vector semantics" are out of date.
- Manning, Raghavan & Schütze: also the pages on stemming and lemmatization and on
  BM25. Free in full.
- Silge & Robinson, *Text Mining with R*: for statisticians who think in data
  frames rather than matrices, its TF-IDF chapter may click faster.
- Hugging Face course: the BPE lesson is the direct sequel to our toy
  implementation.
- tiktoken: the library used for the cost measurements.
- scikit-learn docs: read once properly and most "why don't my numbers match the
  book" questions disappear; its 20 Newsgroups classification example is an
  extended version of our experiment.
- Stanford CS276 (Information Retrieval and Web Search): the public course closest
  to this chapter's scope; CS224N picks up where Chapter 3 begins.
- Elena Voita's NLP Course For You: the clearest visual explanation of the move
  from sparse counts to dense vectors.
:::
